To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the global economy became less carbon efficient between 1997 and 2011, that international trade has a significant effect in the distribution of emissions across countries, and that the distribution of responsibility across countries depends strongly on the choice of the accounting method.

the carbon intensity of production has been decreasing over time, that trade in intermediate inputs has played an important role in the reduction of the carbon intensity of consumption and that, as the carbon intensity of trade has been decreasing over the last decade, trade has contributed positively to the reduction of the global carbon footprint.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What are the main trends in the global carbon footprint of production and consumption over time?
the role of international economic activity and international trade on the global carbon emissions, and the implications of the recent global recession on the global carbon footprint.
the following three questions: How have emissions evolved in different countries and sectors in the period from 1997–2011?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
international trade has been a major contributor to the recent reduction in global CO2 emissions per unit of GDP.
international trade has had a significant impact on carbon emissions in the past two decades and that the global economy has become more carbon efficient.
the global economy became more carbon efficient over the past decade, and this improvement is mainly driven by the increase of trade in intermediate goods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
international trade has played a major role in shaping global carbon dioxide emissions.
the world is getting more carbon efficient and that trade plays a significant role in reducing emissions.
international trade has a strong effect on carbon efficiency, but not on carbon emissions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the role of international emissions embodied in traded goods has grown significantly in recent decades, and is now a substantial part of global emissions, especially for the most carbon-intensive sectors.
international trade has been a key driver of emissions over the past decade, with a growing role in emissions embodied in imports.
the role of international embodied trade in driving global emissions has increased substantially in the last decade, and that the global economy is becoming more carbon efficient.
